Mandatory Background:

1) Understanding Formal Methods by Jean-Francois Monin - This is the absolute best for getting a grip on the breadth, concepts and sample tools for Formal Mathematics/Specification/Verification. Fire-hose of information (not a step-by-step textbook) so use this as a map for everything "Formal". The S/N ratio is very high (~250 pages only!) so use AI/Textbooks to help explain concepts you find difficult to understand.

Practical:

1) Software Abstractions: Logic, Language, and Analysis by Daniel Jackson - Uses "Alloy" language to teach Structural (i.e. Data) Modeling.

2) Specifying Systems: The TLA+ Language and Tools for Hardware and Software Engineers by Leslie Lamport - Uses "TLA+" language to teach Behavioural (i.e. State Machine) modeling.

The above two are for "System Modeling" i.e. everything needed to formally build complete systems.

3) Finally, You should also look at the bunch of free books on the Lean4 website which can be studied parallely for "code-level" proofs and verification.

PS: There are a few more (eg. Event-B method etc.) but you can get to those if/when you need to.

wbeckler · Oct 31, 2026

I think the royal combo is Lean 4/TLA+/etc. plus AI plus a deterministic generator. For large systems formal method assertions need to be compressed down to a human comprehensible size. This can happen when the assertions are confirming the accuracy of a model and its attached code generators. The generator can generate proofs of the generated code and a human only needs to ensure that the generator provably generates the correct mass scale assertions.

This is how formal methods can constrain AI for large systems.

We're doing this at the Open Markets Initiative, where we've generated millions of lines of Lean 4, TLA+, and Rocq that ensure that our open source electronic trading protocol code is accurate. We didn't expect it but the Lean prover did identify some incorrect steps. https://github.com/Open-Markets-Initiative
